# Independent audit of the global ordinary simplex-volume stability reduction

Audited source:
global-ordinary-depth-simplex-volume-stability-root.md.


compactness reduction is valid with the stated local theorem and
ordinary equality rigidity as its dependencies. This audit checks
the normalization, compactness, continuity, equality use, and
transfer to every minimum-volume enclosing simplex. It does not
replace the separate audit of the quantitative local theorem.

## 1. Maximum inscribed simplex and the uniform enclosing polytope

The volume determinant is continuous on \(K^{d+1}\), which is
compact. A full-dimensional body admits a positive-volume
inscribed simplex, so its maximum is positive and attained.
An invertible affine map sends an attaining simplex to the
standard simplex \(T\). It multiplies every relevant volume by
one constant and bijects halfspaces, preserving both maximality
of the inscribed simplex and normalized ordinary depth.

Replacing the \(i\)-th vertex of \(T\) by \(x\in K\) gives an
inscribed simplex of volume \(|\lambda_i(x)|\,|T|\).
The determinant identity holds with either orientation and
also when the replacement simplex is degenerate. Therefore
\(|\lambda_i(x)|\le1\) for all \(i\).
The resulting polytope \(P\) is closed and bounded because
\(\lambda_i=x_i\), \(1\le i\le d\), in the standard frame.
It contains \(T\), and every normalized body lies between
these two fixed sets.

## 2. Closed normalized class and its only simplex member

Hausdorff compactness of convex sets in the fixed bounding
polytope applies. Both inclusions \(T\subseteq K\subseteq P\)
are closed conditions. For a limiting tuple
\(x_0,\ldots,x_d\in K\), Hausdorff convergence supplies
approximating vertices in each \(K_j\). Determinant continuity
then preserves the upper bound \(|T|\) on every inscribed
simplex. Thus the full normalized class is compact and every
member remains full dimensional.

If a member is itself a simplex, its volume is at most
\(|T|\), while containment of \(T\) gives the reverse
inequality. Strict containment of a full-dimensional simplex
in a convex body increases volume: any exterior point and
the violated facet of \(T\) span a positive-volume cone
outside \(T\). Hence the only simplex in the class is \(T\).
No uniqueness of the original maximizing inscribed simplex
is assumed or needed.

## 3. Maximum-depth continuity and the positive far gap

For Hausdorff-convergent convex bodies in this class,
indicators converge at every point outside the limiting
boundary. For an interior point, failure of eventual
containment would yield a sequence of separating supporting
directions and contradict its positive interior-ball margin.
For an exterior point, Hausdorff convergence immediately
gives eventual exclusion. The limiting boundary has zero
ordinary volume, the fixed box dominates all indicators, and
all volumes are at least \(|T|>0\). Consequently normalized
uniform measures converge in total variation.

At every fixed ambient point the two depth functions differ
by at most the same total variation distance, uniformly over
all containing halfspaces. Taking suprema over the entire
ambient space avoids any varying-candidate-set difficulty.
For uniform full-dimensional convex bodies this supremum is
the attained interior maximum used in the source. Thus
\(D(K)\) is continuous on the compact normalized class.

Distance from \(T\) in the Hausdorff-infinity metric is
continuous. The far subclass is therefore compact.
On a nonempty far subclass the nonnegative continuous
function \(D(K)-\Gamma_d\) attains a minimum. If that minimum
were zero, the separately proved ordinary equality rigidity
would make the minimizer a simplex, hence \(T\), contradicting
the positive distance condition. The minimum is strictly
positive. The source explicitly treats the empty subclass
by assigning \(\eta_d=1\); it makes no attainment claim for
an empty class.

This use of rigidity concerns ordinary maximum depth, not
equality of one centroid cap alone. The cited rigidity note
supplies exactly the required implication.

## 4. Combining the near and far cases

In the near case, the normalized body satisfies the fixed
local theorem's Hausdorff hypothesis. Its enclosing-simplex
estimate supplies coefficient \(4/(\Gamma_d c_d)\).
In the far case the positive depth gap and the elementary
bound \(0\le1-|K|/|S|\le1\) supply coefficient \(1/\eta_d\).
The distance boundary may belong to both cases without
affecting either estimate.

Existence of a minimum-volume enclosing simplex is supplied
by the stated enclosing-simplex dependency, whose bounded
vertex argument applies to every full-dimensional body.
The inequality holds for every minimizer. In particular,
even an existential local formulation would suffice for
the volume-ratio conclusion, since all minimum-volume
enclosing simplices have the same volume.
No continuity of the minimizing simplex or its vertices
under arbitrary body variation is needed in the global
argument.

The inverse affine map preserves minimum enclosing volume,
all volume ratios, and ordinary halfspace depth. For nested
uniform bodies, the supremum-set total variation equals
\(1-|K|/|S|\), and cap distance is at most that value.
These facts verify all final comparisons.

The constant is dimension-only and finite; its far-class
term is an attained compact minimum rather than an explicit
formula. Dimension one is correctly separated as the
interval case. No arbitrary affine transformation of a
mixed lattice, and no mixed-integer stability conclusion,
is present.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
